papers.title: Fast Rates for Offline Contextual Bandits with Forward-KL Regularization under Single-Policy Concentrability
papers.abstract: \emph{Kullback-Leibler} (KL) regularization is ubiquitous in reinforcement learning algorithms in the form of \emph{reverse} or \emph{forward} KL. Recent studies have demonstrated $\epsilon^{-1}$-type fast rates for decision making under reverse KL regularization, in contrast to the standard $\epsilon^{-2}$-type sample complexity. However, for forward-KL-regularized objectives, existing statistical analyses are either not applicable or result in $\tilde{O}(\epsilon^{-2})$ slow rates. We take the first step towards addressing this problem via a streamlined analysis of forward-KL-regularized offline CBs. We give the first $\tilde{O}(\epsilon^{-1})$ upper bounds in tabular and general function approximation settings, both under notions of \emph{single-policy concentrability}. In particular, our convex-analytical pipeline unifies these settings by exploiting the pessimism principle in a novel way and completely bypasses the proof routines in previous works based on the mean value theorem, which might be of independent interest. Moreover, we provide rate-optimal lower bounds, manifesting the tightness of our upper bounds in terms of statistical rates. Our lower bounds also demonstrate that the forward-KL-regularized sample complexity recovers the unregularized slow rate in the low-regularization regime, similarly to the reverse-KL regularization.

papers.title: Spectral Thresholds in Correlated Spiked Models and Fundamental Limits of Partial Least Squares
papers.abstract: We provide a rigorous random matrix theory analysis of spiked cross-covariance models where the signals across two high-dimensional data channels are partially aligned. These models are motivated by multi-modal learning and form the standard generative setting underlying Partial Least Squares (PLS), a widely used yet theoretically underdeveloped method. We show that the leading singular values of the sample cross-covariance matrix undergo a Baik-Ben Arous-Peche (BBP)-type phase transition, and we characterize the precise thresholds for the emergence of informative components. Our results yield the first sharp asymptotic description of the signal recovery capabilities of PLS in this setting, revealing a fundamental performance gap between PLS and the Bayes-optimal estimator. In particular, we identify the SNR and correlation regimes where PLS fails to recover any signal, despite detectability being possible in principle. These findings clarify the theoretical limits of PLS and provide guidance for the design of reliable multi-modal inference methods in high dimensions.

papers.title: Counterexamples and Sufficient Conditions: Comments on "Optimally-Transported Generalized Method of Moments"
papers.abstract: We comment on the optimally-transported generalized method of moments (OTGMM) of Schennach and Starck (2026) and give counterexamples to Theorems 2-6. In the small-error analysis, the assumptions do not ensure consistency or asymptotic normality (Theorems 2-3). In the large-error analysis, Theorem 4 states the equivalence between the OTGMM estimator and the GMM estimator with modified moments, and Theorems 5-6 assert consistency and asymptotic normality. Through counterexamples, we show that the equivalence in Theorem 4 fails and a component of the Lagrange multiplier has different limits under the two estimators (Theorems 5-6). We also point out that, under misspecification, the population value selected by OTGMM depends on the metric. We give sufficient conditions and establish results following the original motivation for OTGMM. Our corrections to Theorems 4-6 change their assumptions or interpretation more substantially than those to Theorems 2 and 3. Furthermore, we correct Assumption 16 and the test's null distribution.

papers.title: On statistical inference for non-linear dynamical systems evolving in their global attractor
papers.abstract: We consider a periodic scalar reaction-diffusion system over a two-dimensional domain under natural conditions on the reaction function and with initial condition $\theta$. We show that on the global attractor $\mathcal A$ of the resulting dynamical system $(u_\theta(t):t>0)$, a reverse Poincar\'e inequality holds true, and that as a consequence the map $\theta \mapsto u_\theta(t)$ satisfies an $L^2(\Om)$-Lipschitz stability estimate on $\mathcal A$ for any $t>0$ fixed. We then show that statistical recovery of an initial condition $\theta$ in the attractor $\mathcal A$, as well as prediction of the states $u_\theta$, is possible from discrete measurements of the system at parametric $1/\sqrt N$ convergence rates.

papers.title: Estimating Treatment Effects Through Intermediate-Event Pathways with Multi-State Data
papers.abstract: During clinical trials evaluating a drug's effect on a survival endpoint, intermediate events often occur before the primary event. The treatment can affect the primary event through multiple pathways via intermediate events. With multiple intermediate events, each is a treatment-induced confounder of transitions out of the others, so we cannot identify natural or separable effects. We instead consider stochastic interventions that assign each transition the identifiable observed-history hazard of either arm. Contrasts between the resulting counterfactual cumulative incidences define transition-, event-, and path-targeted effects, identifiable without cross-world or isolation assumptions. Based on the efficient influence functions for the counterfactual cumulative incidences under hypothetical interventions, we construct multiply robust and semiparametrically efficient estimators for these targeted treatment effects. Our proposed framework quantifies treatment effects through each transition, on each event, and along each path. By analyzing data from the LEADER trial, we find that liraglutide significantly reduces the risk of cardiovascular and microvascular events. The reduction in all-cause mortality is primarily mediated by its effects on expanded major adverse cardiovascular events.

papers.title: Validity of the Behrens--Fisher solution
papers.abstract: The Behrens--Fisher fiducial interval for the difference of two normal means is known from the numerical work of Robinson (1976) to be conservative, but a proof has been lacking. The results here prove that the fiducial interval for any linear combination of $k$ normal means has coverage probability at least its nominal level for all values of the unknown variances. Taraldsen (2026) explains this in more detail using the original data of Behrens (1926). The proof presented in the following rests on a novel plug-in inequality: if a threshold function controls a scaled sum of pivots pointwise in the scale vector, then it also controls the sum with the observed scales plugged in, provided the location errors satisfy a concentration condition formulated through a weighted geometric mean. Independent normal errors satisfy the condition.

papers.title: Neyman Orthogonalized Specification Tests for Conditional Tail Index Models
papers.abstract: We develop specification tests for parametric conditional tail index models of heavy-tailed distributions. The tests are based on a projected empirical process that removes the first-order effect of estimating the null parameter. Within the conditional Hall class, we identify conditions under which projection also eliminates the leading Pareto approximation bias in the test process, permitting lower thresholds while preserving asymptotically correct size. We establish the validity of the tests via multiplier bootstrap. For log-linear models, bootstrap validity extends to settings in which covariates among observations above a common threshold concentrate and the smallest eigenvalue of the information matrix tends to zero. We further propose a data-driven threshold selection rule based on an estimate of the Pareto approximation bias after projection. The rule allows lower thresholds to retain more observations for testing while limiting size distortions, with potential gains in power. The finite sample performance of the tests is examined through simulations and a real data application.

papers.title: A Partial-Matching Proof of the Neyman--Pearson Lemma
papers.abstract: Testing seeks to distinguish distributions, whereas matching seeks to identify their common mass. I show that this apparent opposition provides a direct proof of the Neyman--Pearson lemma. Maximal partial matching between the alternative distribution and a scaled null distribution separates them into a common component and two mutually singular residuals. An elementary dual problem then turns this separation into a testing rule: complementary slackness forces rejection on the alternative residual and non-rejection on the scaled-null residual, leaving freedom to randomize at the likelihood-ratio threshold. Thus the optimal test emerges from maximal matching rather than being proposed in advance. The matching profile also determines the optimal power envelope.

papers.title: Sequential Certification of Partially Identified Product Targets: Information Limits and Adaptive Sampling
papers.abstract: We study the cost of certifying a scalar target driven by a product of centered Bernoulli means when an unobserved terminal gate leaves irreducible uncertainty. Each factor can be queried independently at a price. We derive the exact identified interval and determine when a requested accuracy is feasible. At every fixed strictly feasible interior instance, the optimal high-confidence expected cost is $(1+o(1))\log(1/\delta)/D^*$, where $D^*$ is an answer-and-allocation information game; a globally honest procedure attains this benchmark. At product cancellation, we solve the game through a one-dimensional inverse-KL equation and explicit cost weights. For two tickets, quartic projections and rational bounds give checkable global optimality gaps. Joint confidence--precision limits expose a failure of the analyzed fixed pilot: it can cost asymptotically at least twice the optimum. A charged, precision-aware pilot with checkpoint certification restores optimal expected cost in exact arithmetic when $\log\{e+\log(1/g)\}=o(\log(1/\delta))$ for effective precision $g$, including exponential and certain double-exponential precision scales. Pooled rescue preserves validity and cannot increase observation cost on coupled paths. Implemented auditors verify returns by rational inequalities; reproducible experiments show both savings and finite-confidence overhead. These guarantees concern the specified independent-reference model and its scalar target.

papers.title: A Note on the Cut-Locus-Corrected Fr\'echet Mean Central Limit Theorem
papers.abstract: We record two observations concerning \cite{HLW24}. First, the proof of its Theorem~1 yields the population linearization (13)--(14) at \textit{any critical point} of the Fr\'echet function $F_\mu$, under its remaining geometric and measure-theoretic assumptions; neither isolation nor a nonsingular Hessian of $F_\mu$ is needed. Second, its Theorem~2 is given a shorter proof by applying the M-estimator theorem \cite[Theorem~5.23, pp.~53--54]{vdV98} to negative squared distance in normal coordinates, as opposed to the Donsker argument used there. We verify the pointwise differentiability, local square-integrable Lipschitz bound, second order expansion of population loss, consistency, and empirical maximization hypotheses. The resulting covariance retains the cut-locus correction. The same argument applies to suitably selected local sample Fr\'echet minima when the population Hessian is positive definite.

papers.title: Exact regions for the symmetrized Blest coefficient
papers.abstract: Spearman's rho treats all ranks alike, yet in many comparisons of two rankings an agreement at the top matters more than one at the bottom. Blest's rank correlation builds this preference into Spearman's rho, and its symmetrized version $\eta$, introduced by Genest and Plante, does so without favoring either of the two rankings. How far can such a top-weighted coefficient stray from other rank correlations? We answer this question for Spearman's rho, Blomqvist's beta and Chatterjee's rank correlation $\xi$ by determining the exact set of values that $\eta$ and each of these coefficients can attain jointly. Given Spearman's rho, $\eta$ can differ from it by at most $27/128$, and the extreme values of $\eta$ are attained only when the two rankings agree perfectly on the top ranks and are completely reversed on the bottom ranks, or vice versa. Given Blomqvist's beta, $\eta$ obeys exactly the same sharp bounds as Spearman's rho. For Chatterjee's rank correlation, both boundary curves are explicit and are attained by copulas with densities. Here symmetrization has a surprising effect. Compared with Blest's original coefficient, $\eta$ has a narrower range at fixed Spearman's rho, but near independence a wider range at fixed Chatterjee's rank correlation, where $|\eta|$ can come close to $\sqrt{11\xi/5}$ while Blest's coefficient stays below $\sqrt{32\xi/15}$. The proofs combine explicit Kantorovich potentials from optimal transport with a convex relaxation that turns out to be exact.

papers.title: Sharp moderate deviations and uniform Berry--Esseen bounds for Hotelling's $T^2$-statistic via Stein's method
papers.abstract: Let $\mathbf X_1,\ldots,\mathbf X_n$ be independent random vectors in $\mathbb R^d$ with common mean $\boldsymbol\mu_n$, where $d\ge2$ is a fixed integer. Let $\bar{\mathbf X}_n=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbf X_i$ denote the sample mean and let \[ \widehat\Sigma_n=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n (\mathbf X_i-\bar{\mathbf X}_n) (\mathbf X_i-\bar{\mathbf X}_n)^\top \] denote the sample covariance matrix. Assume that the average covariance matrix is positive definite and that $\widehat\Sigma_n$ is nonsingular almost surely. For testing $H_0:\boldsymbol\mu_n=\boldsymbol\mu_0$, the Hotelling statistic is \[ T^2_{H,n} =n(\bar{\mathbf X}_n-\boldsymbol\mu_0)^\top \widehat\Sigma_n^{-1} (\bar{\mathbf X}_n-\boldsymbol\mu_0). \] Under $H_0$, we establish finite-sample Cram\'er-type moderate deviation results and uniform Berry--Esseen bounds under finite $p$th moments for $2<p\le3$. The moderate deviation error order is optimal over independent triangular arrays, as shown by explicit constructions. For identically distributed observations with a fixed distribution, we obtain \[ \sup_{0\le x\le b_n} \left| \frac{\mathbb P(T^2_{H,n}\ge x^2)} {\mathbb P(\chi_d^2\ge x^2)}-1 \right| = O\!\left((1+b_n)^p n^{-(p-2)/2}\right) \] for every nonnegative sequence $b_n=o(n^{(p-2)/(2p)})$. The uniform Berry--Esseen bound is $O(n^{-(p-2)/2})$. The proof uses a radial Stein identity and a recursive error estimate. We apply the results to chi-squared calibration in simultaneous testing.

papers.title: Beyond Maximum Likelihood: Variational Inequality Estimation for Generalized Linear Models
papers.abstract: Generalized linear models (GLMs) are fundamental tools for statistical modeling, with maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) serving as the classical approach for parameter inference. While MLE performs well for canonical GLMs, it can become computationally challenging in more general settings with non-canonical, non-smooth, or saturating link functions, where the resulting optimization landscape may be ill-conditioned, non-convex, or non-differentiable. In this paper, we study an alternative estimation framework based on variational inequalities (VIs), which formulates GLM estimation through an operator-based equilibrium condition rather than likelihood minimization. We analyze the VI estimator from a statistical perspective and establish finite-sample error bounds and asymptotic normality, together with convergence guarantees for fixed-point and stochastic approximation algorithms. The framework accommodates a broad class of link functions, including non-canonical, non-smooth, and non-monotone cases satisfying a strong Minty-type condition, and extends naturally to generalized additive models (GAMs) via basis expansion. Numerical experiments demonstrate that under a fixed iteration budget, the VI approach achieves competitive estimation accuracy and faster, more stable convergence than MLE, particularly in GLMs and GAMs with non-canonical or non-smooth link functions.

papers.title: High-dimensional Gaussian Graphical Model Testing for Long-Memory Time Series
papers.abstract: Many real-world high-dimensional time series exhibit long-memory, but Gaussian graphical model testing in this regime remains understudied. We develop a direct, data-adaptive test statistic for assessing conditional independence in the graph structure of stationary Gaussian time series. We establish a finite-sample, Berry--Esseen type Gaussian approximation bound for the statistic, which applies to both short-memory and long-memory time series. The testing procedure uses a block bootstrap method, on which we provide a finite-sample validity result including in the ultra-high-dimensional scenario, and can be extended to comparing graphical structures in two-sample tests. We also develop a consistency-empowered correction to the statistic and show that such tests attain asymptotic consistency in both size and power. Our proposed method is applied to real-world fMRI data to understand functional connectivities within brain in different periods.

papers.title: Decentralized Sparse Quantile Regression
papers.abstract: Distributed statistical learning has recently attracted significant attention owing to its computational efficiency and scalability in large-scale systems. However, the non-smooth quantile loss poses substantial challenges to the development of efficient decentralized algorithms for quantile regression. Existing methods may either suffer from slow convergence or rely on smoothing-based approximations that require additional stringent assumptions, particularly in high-dimensional settings. To address these issues, we propose a decentralized framework that integrates gradient tracking with iterative hard thresholding for sparse quantile estimation. The proposed method avoids smoothing approximations and relaxes the initialization requirement. Theoretically, we show that the proposed algorithm achieves linear convergence under stated regularity conditions and that the resulting estimator attains the same order of statistical accuracy as its centralized counterpart. We further develop a decentralized information criterion for selecting the working sparsity level and establish support screening guarantees. Numerical experiments and a real-data study illustrate the finite-sample performance of the proposed method.

papers.title: Hyper Input Convex Neural Networks for Shape Constrained Learning and Optimal Transport
papers.abstract: We introduce Hyper Input Convex Neural Networks (HyCNNs), a novel neural network architecture designed for learning convex functions. HyCNNs combine the principles of Maxout networks with input convex neural networks (ICNNs) to create a neural network that is always convex in the input, theoretically capable of leveraging depth, and performs reliably when trained at scale compared to ICNNs. Concretely, we prove that HyCNNs require exponentially fewer parameters than ICNNs to approximate quadratic functions up to a given precision. Throughout a series of synthetic experiments, we demonstrate that HyCNNs outperform existing ICNNs and MLPs in terms of predictive performance for convex regression and interpolation tasks. We further apply HyCNNs to learn high-dimensional optimal transport maps for synthetic examples and for single-cell data, where they oftentimes outperform ICNN-based neural optimal transport methods and other baselines across a wide range of setting.

papers.title: Higher-Order Neyman Orthogonality in Moment-Condition Models
papers.abstract: We construct moment functions that are Neyman-orthogonal to a chosen order in moment-condition models that involve finite-dimensional nuisance parameters. These moment functions reduce sensitivity to estimation error in the nuisance parameters and, as such, offer a unified and tractable route to higher-order debiasing in a wide range of econometric models. The number of additional nuisance parameters required by our construction, beyond those already present in the original moment conditions, is independent of the order of orthogonalization and can be reduced to a single scalar if desired.

papers.title: Nonparametric Bandits with Single-Index Rewards: Optimality and Adaptivity
papers.abstract: Contextual bandits are a central framework for sequential decision-making, with applications ranging from recommendation systems to clinical trials. While nonparametric methods can flexibly model complex reward structures, they suffer from the curse of dimensionality. We address this challenge using a single-index model, which projects high-dimensional covariates onto a one-dimensional subspace while preserving nonparametric flexibility. We first develop a nonasymptotic theory for offline single-index regression for each arm, combining maximum rank correlation for index estimation with local polynomial regression. Building on this foundation, we propose a single-index bandit algorithm and establish its convergence rate. We further derive a matching lower bound, showing that the algorithm achieves minimax-optimal regret independent of the ambient dimension $d$, thereby overcoming the curse of dimensionality. We also establish an impossibility result for adaptation: without additional assumptions, no policy can adapt to unknown smoothness levels. Under a standard self-similarity condition, however, we construct a policy that remains minimax-optimal while automatically adapting to the unknown smoothness. Finally, as the dimension $d$ increases, our algorithm continues to achieve minimax-optimal regret, revealing a phase transition that characterizes the fundamental limits of single-index bandit learning.

papers.title: Second-order PACF asymptotics and discrimination between fractional Gaussian noise and $\FARIMA(0,d,0)$
papers.abstract: Fractional Gaussian noise and $\FARIMA(0,d,0)$ have the same long-memory pole $|\theta|^{-2d}$ and hence the same leading PACF law $\alpha(n)\sim d/n$. We show that this agreement breaks at the first non-universal order. For $0<d<1/2$, the pure fGn PACF satisfies $$ \alpha_{\fGn}(n)=\frac d n+\frac{C_{\fGn}(d)}{n^2}+o(n^{-2}), \qquad C_{\fGn}(d)<d^2, $$ The proof uses the Bingham--Inoue--Kasahara representation, a phase-coefficient expansion for fGn, and a Hankel-operator perturbation argument. Thus the fGn spectral envelope is invisible at first order but visible in second-order finite prediction, explaining why short-memory order selection can differ when fGn data are fitted by FARIMA-type models.

papers.title: U-centering as subset ANOVA: edge regression and higher-order theory
papers.abstract: Unbiased squared distance covariance and the Hilbert-Schmidt independence criterion (HSIC) are fourth-order U-statistics, yet U-centering evaluates them from pairwise arrays in $O(n^2)$ operations. We show that U-centering is exactly least-squares residualization after fitting additive endpoint effects. This analysis of variance (ANOVA) interpretation explains the zero row sums and the normalization through residual degrees of freedom. The same geometry gives regression representations of dependence and two-sample statistics, exact permutation variances, and relations among pooled and regression mean squares. For arrays indexed by $r$-element subsets and $n\ge2r$, higher-order U-centering removes all lower-order subset effects and projects onto a space of dimension $\binom{n}{r}-\binom{n}{r-1}$. For fixed symmetric square-integrable kernels evaluated on independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) paired observations, we derive the residual covariance matrix, exact mean-squared errors for estimating the highest-order Hoeffding components, unbiased positive semidefinite (PSD) covariance estimates, and moment formulas under independence and permutation. The normalized residual inner product equals a direct unbiased estimator involving up to $2r$ observations, but can be evaluated in $O(n^r)$ operations for fixed $r$. For four-argument matching kernels, three matrix products yield exactly unbiased estimators of a fourth spectral moment of kernel cross-covariance in $O(n^3)$ arithmetic and $O(n^2)$ storage. A numerical illustration distinguishes dependence structures with equal HSIC and different spectral concentration.
